result.label: Indicator - Labour productivity
note:
[b]Labour productivity[/b]

[b]How do we measure this?[/b]
Productivity is measured by dividing total economic output (Gross Value Added) by total hours worked in the economy. Data is expressed in index format and adjusted for inflation by fixing prices for all years to the prevailing price levels of a reference year. In the latest edition of the estimates this price reference year is 2022 (i.e. 2022 = 100).[b] [/b]Note, that the Price Reference Year is distinct from the comparison year.

[b]Source[/b]
Subregional productivity: labour productivity indices by UK ITL2 and ITL3 subregions - Office for National Statistics
[url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/labourproductivity/datasets/subregionalproductivitylabourproductivitygvaperhourworkedandgvaperfilledjobindicesbyuknuts2andnuts3subregions]Sub-Regional Labour Productivity, Office for National Statistics[/url]

[b]Impact of Covid-19[/b]
The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic was unevenly distributed across sectors of the economy. Lower productivity industries such as hospitality and food service saw a significant fall in their share of total hours worked between 2019 and 2021 while higher productivity industries such as Banking and Finance increased their shares of total hours worked. At the same time, the share of hours worked by those with tertiary qualifications increased by 8.5ppts between 2019 and 2021, reflecting the fact that higher skilled occupations were generally more adaptable to remote working. These temporary compositional shifts produced a significant upward effect on productivity estimates in 2020 and 2021. The decline in productivity from the high point seen in 2021 in part reflects a return towards pre-COVID compositional norms.

[b]Further information[/b]
1. Output per hour worked is widely recognised as the conceptually best measure of productivity, particularly when making comparisons between different regions as this indicator better accounts for differences in factors such as participation rates and differential mixes of full / part time employment.
2. Northern Ireland has consistently lagged UK average productivity. While this gap has narrowed somewhat over the last 20 years (in 2004 NI output per hour worked was 18.8% lower than the equivalent UK average) as of 2023 it remains significant (12.4% lower than the UK average in 2023).
